title: Part 4, Chapter 3
paragraphs: The fact was that up to the very last moment he had never expected such an outcome. He had been overbearing to the end, never dreaming that two destitute and defenseless women could escape his control. This conviction was reinforced by his vanity and self-regard—a conceit that bordered on delusion. Pyotr Petrovitch, who had risen from nothing, was morbidly prone to self-admiration, had the highest opinion of his intelligence, and sometimes even gloated over his reflection in the mirror. But what he loved and valued above all was the money he had accumulated through hard work and every means available: that money made him the equal of everyone who had once been his superior.

When he had bitterly reminded Dounia that he'd resolved to take her despite evil rumors, Pyotr Petrovitch had spoken with perfect sincerity and had genuinely felt indignant at such 'black ingratitude.' Yet when he first proposed to Dounia, he was fully aware that the gossip was groundless. The story had been contradicted everywhere by Marfa Petrovna and was by then disbelieved by the whole town, which warmly defended Dounia. He would not have denied knowing all this. Yet he still prized his own magnanimity in raising Dounia to his level and considered it something heroic. In speaking of it to Dounia, he had revealed the secret feeling he nursed and admired, and he could not understand why others failed to admire it too. He had called on Raskolnikov with the feelings of a benefactor about to reap the fruits of his good deeds and hear flattering praise. And as he went downstairs now, he felt himself to be a most undeservedly injured and unappreciated man.

Dounia was simply essential to him; giving her up was unthinkable. For years he had entertained voluptuous dreams of marriage while continuing to save money. He brooded with relish, in deepest secrecy, over the image of a girl—virtuous, poor (she must be poor), very young, very pretty, well-born and well-educated, very timid, one who had suffered greatly and was utterly humbled before him, one who would look up to him her whole life as her savior, worship him, admire him, and him alone. How many scenes, how many romantic episodes he had imagined on this seductive theme, when his day's work was done! And now the dream of so many years was nearly realized. The beauty and education of Avdotya Romanovna had impressed him; her helpless situation was powerfully attractive. He had found even more than he'd dreamed of—here was a girl of pride, character, virtue, education, and breeding superior to his own (he felt that), and this creature would be slavishly grateful for his heroic condescension all her life, humbling herself in the dust before him, while he wielded absolute, boundless power over her! Not long before, after much reflection and hesitation, he had also made an important career change and was now entering a wider sphere of business. With this move, his cherished dreams of climbing into a higher social class seemed about to come true. He was determined to try his luck in Petersburg. He knew that women could accomplish a great deal. The charm of a beautiful, virtuous, educated woman might smooth his path enormously, attracting people, creating an aura around him—and now it was all in ruins! This sudden, terrible rupture struck like a thunderbolt; it was like a grotesque joke, an absurdity. He had only been the tiniest bit imperious, hadn't even had time to speak his mind, had merely made a joke, gotten carried away—and it had ended so disastrously. And, of course, he did love Dounia in his way; he already possessed her in his dreams—and all at once! No! The very next day it must all be put right, smoothed over, settled. Above all, that conceited puppy who had caused it all must be crushed. With a sick feeling he also recalled Razumihin, but quickly reassured himself on that score: as though a fellow like that could be compared to him! The one he truly feared was Svidrigaïlov. In short, he had a great deal to attend to.

"No, I'm the most to blame!" said Dounia, kissing and embracing her mother. "I was tempted by his money, but on my honor, brother, I had no idea he was such a despicable man. If I'd seen through him sooner, nothing would have tempted me! Don't blame me, brother!"
"God has delivered us! God has delivered us!" Pulcheria Alexandrovna murmured, half-consciously, as though not fully grasping what had happened.

They were all relieved, and within five minutes they were laughing. Only now and then Dounia went pale and frowned, remembering what had passed. Pulcheria Alexandrovna was surprised to find she was relieved too; only that morning, a break with Luzhin had seemed like a catastrophe. Razumihin was overjoyed. He didn't yet dare express his happiness fully, but he was trembling with excitement, as though a tremendous weight had been lifted from his chest. Now he had the right to devote his life to them, to serve them. Anything might happen now! But he was afraid to think about further possibilities and didn't dare let his imagination run. Raskolnikov, however, sat in the same spot, almost sullen and indifferent. Though he had been the most insistent about getting rid of Luzhin, he now seemed the least affected by what had happened. Dounia couldn't help thinking he was still angry with her, and Pulcheria Alexandrovna watched him anxiously.
"What did Svidrigaïlov say to you?" Dounia asked, coming up to him.
"Yes, yes!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
Raskolnikov raised his head.
"He wants to give you ten thousand roubles, and he wishes to see you once, in my presence."
"See her! Out of the question!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna. "And how dare he offer her money!"
Raskolnikov then repeated—rather drily—his conversation with Svidrigaïlov, leaving out the account of Marfa Petrovna's ghostly visits, not wanting unnecessary digressions.
"What answer did you give him?" Dounia asked.

"At first I said I wouldn't bring you any message. Then he said he'd do his best to see you on his own, without my help. He assured me his passion for you was a passing fancy and that he no longer has any feelings for you. He doesn't want you to marry Luzhin. His talk was rather muddled on the whole."
"How do you explain him, Rodya? What was your impression?"

"I must confess I don't quite understand him. He offers you ten thousand but says he's not well off. He says he's going away, and ten minutes later forgets he said it. Then he says he's about to get married and already has a bride picked out. He certainly has a motive, probably a bad one. But it's strange how clumsy he is about it, if he really has designs on you. Of course, I refused the money on your behalf, once and for all. Altogether I found him very strange. One might almost think he's mad. But I could be wrong—it might just be a role he's playing. The death of Marfa Petrovna seems to have shaken him deeply."

"God rest her soul," Pulcheria Alexandrovna exclaimed. "I shall always pray for her! Where would we be now, Dounia, without these three thousand? It's as though it fell from heaven! Why, Rodya, this morning we had only three roubles left, and Dounia and I were planning to pawn her watch just to avoid borrowing from that man until he offered help."
Dounia seemed strangely struck by Svidrigaïlov's offer. She stood deep in thought.
"He has some terrible plan," she said in a half-whisper, almost to herself, nearly shuddering.
Raskolnikov noticed her disproportionate alarm.
"I think I'll have to see him again more than once," he said to Dounia.

"We'll keep watch! I'll track him down!" Razumihin cried energetically. "I won't let him out of my sight. Rodya gave me permission himself. He said to me just now: 'Take care of my sister.' Will you give me permission too, Avdotya Romanovna?"
Dounia smiled and held out her hand, but the anxious look didn't leave her face. Pulcheria Alexandrovna watched her timidly, though the three thousand roubles had clearly had a soothing effect.
A quarter of an hour later, they were all engrossed in lively conversation. Even Raskolnikov listened for a while, though he didn't speak. Razumihin held the floor.

"And why, why should you leave?" he rattled on ecstatically. "What would you do in a small town? The important thing is that you're all together and you need each other—you do need each other, believe me! For a while at least. Take me as a partner, and I promise we'll start a wonderful business. I'll explain the whole project in detail—it all came to me this morning, before anything happened. Here's the thing: I have an uncle—I must introduce you to him, a most obliging and respectable old fellow. This uncle has a capital of a thousand roubles, and he lives on his pension and doesn't need the money. For two years he's been pestering me to borrow it from him at six percent interest. I know what that means—he simply wants to help me. Last year I didn't need it, but this year I decided to borrow it as soon as he arrived. You lend me another thousand from your three, and we have enough for a start. So we'll go into partnership—and what are we going to do?"

Then Razumihin laid out his plan. He explained at length that nearly all our publishers and booksellers have no idea what they're selling, which is why they make poor publishers, and that any decent publication generally pays well and sometimes yields a considerable profit. Publishing was what Razumihin had been dreaming of. He'd spent two years working in publishing offices and knew three European languages well, though he'd told Raskolnikov six days earlier that he was 'hopeless' in German—that had been a ploy to get him to take on half a translation and half the payment. He'd been lying, and Raskolnikov knew it.

"Why should we let this chance slip when we have the most important thing—our own capital?" Razumihin cried enthusiastically. "Of course there'll be a lot of work, but we'll work. You, Avdotya Romanovna, Rodion, and I. Some books make excellent profit these days! And the main advantage is that we'll know exactly what needs translating. We'll translate, publish, and learn all at the same time. I can help because I have experience. For nearly two years I've been running around publishers' offices and I know every detail of the trade. You don't have to be a saint to make pots, believe me! And why should we pass up this chance? I know of two or three books where just the idea of translating them is worth a hundred roubles. And I wouldn't take five hundred for the concept of one of them. Yet if I told a publisher, I'm sure he'd hesitate—they're such blockheads! As for the business side—printing, paper, sales—leave that to me. I know my way around. We'll start small and go big. At the very least we'll earn a living and get our investment back."
Dounia's eyes were shining.
"I like what you're saying, Dmitri Prokofitch!" she said.

"I know nothing about it, of course," Pulcheria Alexandrovna put in. "It may be a good idea, but then again, God knows. It's new and untried. Of course, we must stay here at least for a while." She looked at Rodya.
"What do you think, brother?" said Dounia.

"I think it's a very good idea," he answered. "It's too early to dream of a publishing firm, of course, but we could certainly bring out five or six books and be sure of success. I know of one myself that would do well. And as for his being able to manage it, there's no doubt. He knows the business. But we can discuss that later."

"Hurrah!" cried Razumihin. "Now, wait—there's an apartment here in this very building, same landlord. It's separate, doesn't connect with these rooms, it's furnished, and the rent is reasonable—three rooms. Take it for now! I'll pawn the watch tomorrow and bring you the money, and everything can be arranged. You can all live together, with Rodya nearby. But where are you off to, Rodya?"
"What, Rodya, you're leaving already?" Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked in dismay.
"At a moment like this?" Razumihin cried.
Dounia looked at her brother with incredulous astonishment. He held his cap in his hand, preparing to go.

"Anyone would think you were burying me or saying goodbye forever," he said somewhat oddly. He tried to smile, but it didn't quite come off. "But who knows, perhaps it really is the last time we'll see each other," he let slip accidentally. He had been thinking it, and it simply came out.
"What's wrong with you?" his mother cried.
"Where are you going, Rodya?" Dounia asked strangely.
"I'm obliged to," he answered vaguely, as though hesitating over what to say. But there was a look of sharp determination in his white face.

"I was going to say—on my way here—I meant to tell you, mother, and you, Dounia, that it would be better for us to part for a while. I feel unwell, I'm not at peace. I'll come later—I'll come on my own, when I can. I think of you and I love you. Leave me alone. I decided this before—I'm absolutely resolved on it. Whatever happens to me, whether I'm destroyed or not, I want to be alone. Forget me completely. It's better. Don't ask about me. When I can, I'll come or send for you. Maybe it will all work out. But for now, if you love me, let me go—otherwise I'll start to hate you, I can feel it. Goodbye!"
"Good God!" cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna. Both his mother and sister were terribly alarmed. So was Razumihin.
"Rodya, Rodya, make peace with us! Let's be as we were!" his poor mother begged.
He turned slowly to the door and walked out of the room. Dounia caught up with him.
"Brother, what are you doing to mother?" she whispered, her eyes blazing with indignation.
He looked at her dully.
"It doesn't matter—I'll come back. I'm coming," he muttered in an undertone, as though not fully conscious of what he was saying, and went out.
"Heartless, selfish egoist!" Dounia cried.

"He isn't heartless—he's insane! Can't you see? It's you who are heartless, saying that!" Razumihin whispered hotly in her ear, gripping her hand. "I'll be right back!" he shouted to the horror-stricken mother, and ran out.
Raskolnikov was waiting for him at the end of the corridor.
"I knew you'd come after me," he said. "Go back to them—be with them. Be with them tomorrow and always. I—perhaps I'll come, if I can. Goodbye."
And without offering his hand, he walked away.
"But where are you going? What's happening to you? What's wrong? How can you behave like this?" Razumihin muttered, completely at a loss.
Raskolnikov stopped once more.
"Once and for all—never ask me about anything. I have nothing to tell you. Don't come to see me. Maybe I'll come here. Leave me alone, but don't leave them. Do you understand?"

It was dark in the corridor. They stood near a lamp. For a minute they looked at each other in silence. Razumihin remembered that minute for the rest of his life. Raskolnikov's burning, intent eyes grew more penetrating with every second, piercing into his soul, into his consciousness. Suddenly Razumihin started. Something strange passed between them. Some idea, some hint slipped through—something terrible, hideous, and suddenly understood by both. Razumihin went white as a sheet.
"Do you understand now?" Raskolnikov said, his face twitching. "Go back, go to them," he added suddenly, and turning quickly, he walked out of the house.

I shall not try to describe how Razumihin returned to the ladies, how he soothed them, how he insisted that Rodya needed rest during his illness, that Rodya would certainly come back, that he'd come every day, that he was very much upset and mustn't be irritated, that he, Razumihin, would watch over him, find him a doctor—the best doctor—arrange a consultation. In short, from that evening on, Razumihin took his place with them as a son and a brother.
